title: KDA backward, nine stages
formula: d(q, k, v, g, beta, h0) of chunked Kimi Delta Attention with a per-(token, channel) log2 gate and a chunk-local inverse-triangular solve, L=64 chunk, K=V=128, BF16 [B,T,H,128] queries/keys and [B,T,HV,128] values in and out, FP32 accumulation
study_for: How to contract a decay-weighted pairwise term without ever building the decay matrix. `finalize_pre` writes `q_scaled = q * exp2(g_cumsum - g_last)` and `kg = k * exp2(g_last - g_cumsum)` -- reciprocal scalings, one of which reaches 1e25 while the other stays under 1 -- so `finalize_pair` can do the whole O(L^2) intra-chunk pairing as four plain cube matmuls and `finalize_post` multiplies the reciprocal scale straight back in. It is the central trick of this backward and it costs something real: see the note beside `finalize_pair.qk_right` in main.py's TOLERANCE for what an intermediate spanning 1e13 orders of magnitude does to an elementwise comparison.

What the nine launches are for. Read the section banners in kernel.py in order: `finalize_pair` has no vector code at all (four matmuls, 56 lines), while `inverse_epilogue`, `finalize_pre`, `finalize_post` and `finalize_reduce` have no cube at all. The split is the cube/vector alternation, not an arbitrary decomposition -- each boundary is a point where the work changes pipe, and `main.py`'s `execute` is the only place the whole ABI between them is written down.

Two references that disagree on purpose, and a demo that runs both. `reference` differentiates the unrounded fp32 forward with autograd; `reference_stages` models the bf16 and fp32 seams the kernels actually use. That is why `--stages` measures the kernels and the default run measures the algorithm, and why `dk` and `dg` are the only outputs with relaxed residual ceilings (0.15 and 0.25): the saved cumulative gate is stored bf16, so a log2 value can move by up to 0.25 before `exp2` is applied, which lands directly on a multiplicative derivative.

Where an all-bf16 ABI still keeps fp32 in GM. Every public input, every saved forward cache and every public gradient here is bf16, with exactly two exceptions, and both are accumulation points: `inverse_epilogue` emits `dbeta` as fp32 [B,T,HV], and `finalize_post` emits `dq_hv`/`dk_hv` as fp32 [B,HV,C,64,128] which `finalize_reduce` sums over the HV group before rounding to bf16. Rounding either one early loses the group sum.
do_not_copy_when: Your gate is a natural exponential. KDA's gate is base 2 throughout: `g` is scaled by 1/ln(2) into `g_cumsum` and every decay is `exp2`. A stage lifted into an `exp()` pipeline gives a plausible wrong answer instead of failing, which is what the `gentle_decay` case exists to catch -- a shallow decay makes the disagreement visible where a steep one buries it.

Your chunk length is not 64 or K/V is not 128, or T is not a multiple of 64. There is no partial-chunk path. The authored scope is L=64, K=V=128, T=C*64, and the [B,HV,C,64,128] to [B,HV,T,128] view punning that main.py's `execute` does between finalize_pre, finalize_pair and finalize_post is only free because those shapes are the same bytes.

You want the delta rule without a per-channel gate. KDA's gate is per (token, channel) -- a full [B,T,HV,128] tensor, not one value per token. gdn_bwd is the per-token-gate version and delta_rule_bwd is the ungated one; both are much shorter reads and neither needs this unit's nine launches.

You want to lift one kernel out and use it alone. Nothing here is standalone: `finalize_pair` consumes M_qk/M_base/M_beta and the three scaled products exactly as `finalize_pre` laid them out, `inverse_dakk_fused` reads D_tri through a [B,HV,T,64] view of a [B,HV,C,64,64] tensor, and `inverse_mm`'s third output is negated by the caller rather than by the kernel. Those conventions live in main.py's `execute`, and a kernel taken out of it drops them silently.
